title: architecture-standards-guidelines-and-adrs-2026-07-15
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This consolidated guidance document captures Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and standards for API design, coding conventions, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also records recent Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) through mid-2026 that affect cross-team implementation. Treat this page as the single-source-of-truth for service-level standards and ADRs; link specific implementation pages for team-level details.

Goals
- Ensure consistent developer experience across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Make services reliable and observable with clear SLOs and tooling expectations.
- Reduce operational surprises by standardizing request/response contracts, deployment patterns, and performance testing.
- Record and surface trade-offs in ADRs so future maintainers understand prior decisions.

Audience and scope
- Primary audience: backend engineers, platform, SRE, and infra.
- Scope: public/internal REST/gRPC APIs, service code style, infra provisioning and networking, model-serving runtime contracts, telemetry/logging/exporting, and performance SLOs.

1) API Standards
Purpose: consistent, stable, and backward-compatible API interfaces for customers and internal services.

Core rules:
- Versioning: All external-facing APIs must use explicit versioning in the path (e.g., /v1/...). Internal-to-internal gRPC services must use package-level versioning.
- Resource modeling: Use plural nouns for resource URLs (/v1/models/, /v1/deployments/). Actions that mutate state should use POST to a subresource (/v1/deployments/{id}/scale).
- Idempotency: Long-running operations must return an Operation resource with an operation_id and support GET /v1/operations/{id}. Clients may retry idempotently using operation_id.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination with opaque next_cursor. Avoid offset-based pagination for model lists. Example: {"next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ==", "items": [...]} 
- Streaming: Streaming generation APIs must use chunked transfer encoding (HTTP/1.1) or HTTP/2 streaming with a consistent chunk framing. Streaming responses must include: event: token, role, delta; final: done=true. See the "Streaming generation example" snippet below.
- Error responses: JSON error envelope {"code": "INTERNAL", "message": "...", "details": [...]}. Use HTTP semantics: 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors. Provide an error_id for correlation.
- Security: All external APIs require mutual TLS (customer-facing marketplace can use token + mTLS depending on contract). All requests must be authenticated with short-lived tokens; rotation and revocation are documented in security-and-compliance.

Streaming generation example:
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream

event: token
data: {"delta": "hello"}

event: token
data: {"delta": " world"}

event: done
data: {"finish_reason": "stop"}
```

2) Coding standards
Purpose: maintainable, testable, and performant code across services.

Language-specific guidelines (summary):
- Python: target 3.10+, follow PEP8 but prefer explicit typing (mypy, typeshed). Use black for formatting and ruff for linting. All services must include a static type check step in CI.
- Go: go1.20+, idiomatic error handling, no generics in heavy hot-path code unless benched. gofmt + go vet + golangci-lint in CI.
- Rust (runtime components): use edition 2021, enforce clippy warnings as errors for critical crates.

General rules:
- Small functions: keep public function length < 80 lines where practical.
- Defensive programming: validate external input at boundaries.
- Secrets: never check in secrets; use vault/KMS.
- Testing: unit tests for business logic, integration tests for API contracts. All services must provide a basic performance smoke test (see performance section).
- Dependency policy: prefer semver pinned dependencies in production artifacts. Security team approval required for native libs with binary distributions.

3) Infrastructure standards
Purpose: predictable, secure, and repeatable infra provisioning for hosted and private deployments.

Provisioning and IaC:
- Terraform is the canonical IaC for cloud-managed deployments. Modules live in infra/terraform-modules and must be versioned.
- Cross-account/cloud: implement least-privilege IAM roles; prefer role chaining through short-lived STS tokens.
- Network: use VPC peering or private link for control plane to dedicated/private deployment connectivity. Public-facing endpoints must be behind WAF and CDN.

Deployment patterns:
- Blue/green or canary: all production changes must support a canary deployment with traffic split (default 5% canary for 24 hours before increasing).
- Autoscaling: CPU/GPU-based scaling policies plus queue-length soft-scaling for bursty traffic.

Capacity and cost controls:
- Reserved pools: Dedicated customers must be served from reserved GPU pools with autoscaler caps configured by the sales contract.
- Budget alerts: cloud spend per account must trigger PagerDuty when monthly forecast exceeds 80% of committed spend.

4) Model-serving standards
Purpose: ensure consistent runtime behavior, predictable latency, and safety across model types.

Serving contract:
- Model bundle format: models must provide manifest.json with fields: name, version, architecture, tokenizer, kv_cache_compatible, quantization_support. (Teams should mirror the manifest format in model-onboarding docs.)
- API contract: All inference engines expose a standard /infer endpoint (internal) and map to front-door APIs using the Adapter pattern. The adapter must transform the stable REST contract to runtime-specific calls.
- Fallbacks: Every served model must list compatible fallback variants (lower precision, smaller model family) in the manifest. Smart routing will use these for graceful degradation.

Quantization and kernels:
- Default quantization profile for production: int8 for non-safety-critical models with verified bit-level validation. int4 may be used experimentally behind feature flags and must be gated by evaluation harness passing quality thresholds.
- Kernel selection: runtime should select optimized kernels (cuBLAS, CUTLASS, custom CUDA) based on model size and hardware. Add kernel selector metrics to telemetry (see observability).

Safety and content filtering:
- Every model endpoint must run a lightweight safety classifier pre-filter (reject/flag) and a post-generation scoring pass for high-risk customers.

5) Observability standards
Purpose: enable fast detection, triage, and RCA for service and model regressions.

Telemetry requirements:
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry (OTel) distributed traces with 100% sampling for requests > 500ms, 1% sampling for sub-500ms by default. Traces must include: request_id, model_name, model_version, route, region, and kernel_id.
- Metrics: Expose Prometheus metrics for request_latency_ms (histogram), tokens_generated_per_request (counter), kv_cache_hit_ratio (gauge), batch_size_distribution (histogram), and kernel_switch_count (counter).
- Logs: Structured JSON logs at INFO/ERROR; include request_id, operation, user_tier, and anonymized prompt hash. PII must be redacted before logging.
- Alerting: Out-of-the-box SRE alert rules: high_error_rate (>1% 5-minute errors), tail_latency_p99 > 1.5x target, kv_cache_hit_ratio < 0.6 for stateful loads.

Tracing and correlation example:
- Header: X-Request-ID: 01F8XYZ...
- Trace spans: api.gateway -> adapter -> runtime.worker -> kv.cache -> kernel.execute

6) Performance standards and SLOs
Purpose: define acceptable latency, throughput, and cost targets for production services.

SLO tiers (examples):
- Gold (enterprise SLA): p95 latency < 200ms for short prompts (<64 tokens); p99 < 600ms. Error budget 99.95% availability.
- Standard (hosted): p95 < 400ms; p99 < 1s. Error budget 99.9%.
- Private/dedicated: contract-defined but follow same measurement methodology.

Benchmarking and perf tests:
- Perf harness: every model and deployment variant must run the benchmark suite covering cold-starts, streaming throughput, and long-context memory usage. Results stored in benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Acceptance: new runtime changes that affect hot-path code must show performance regression < 5% on p95 in nightly benchmarks or be accompanied by a mitigation plan.

Operational playbooks (summary)
- Degradation detection: if p99 or error rate breach occurs, run the triage checklist: 1) identify impacted routes/models, 2) check autoscaler and capacity, 3) validate kernel/library versions, 4) roll back recent commits if correlated, 5) activate fallback routing to compatible model variant.
- Rollback: maintain a tested rollback artifact for each release; rollbacks should be automated and exercised quarterly.

7) ADRs (recorded decisions)
This section records recently-approved architecture decisions. Each ADR includes rationale, consequences, and owners.

- ADR-2026-01: Stable inference API contract (/v1/generate)
  - Decision: Standardize on a single REST API surface /v1/generate for streaming and non-streaming generation, with an adapter layer for protocol translations (gRPC, websocket).
  - Rationale: Simplifies client SDKs and reduces duplication across hosted/dedicated/private offerings.
  - Consequence: All runtime adaptors must implement adapter contract. SDKs will rely on stable payload fields (prompt, max_tokens, temperature, functions).
  - Owner: eng-developer-experience.

- ADR-2026-02: Default int8 quantization with validation harness
  - Decision: Use int8 as the default production quantization profile where supported; int4 is allowed only behind experiment flags after meeting eval thresholds.
  - Rationale: int8 has mature toolchain support and predictable accuracy/latency tradeoffs.
  - Consequence: Model onboarding must include quantization validation artifacts and bit-level checksums.
  - Owner: applied-ml-and-evals.

- ADR-2026-03: OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing + 1% adaptive sampling
  - Decision: Adopt OTel for traces and metrics with adaptive sampling rules to keep trace storage costs bounded.
  - Rationale: Vendor-neutral standard and ecosystem tools for distributed systems.
  - Consequence: All services must add OTel spans to critical hot-paths before feature is promoted to production.
  - Owner: eng-sre.

- ADR-2026-04: Canary-first deployment policy
  - Decision: Require canary deployments for all user-facing services; default canary traffic 5% for 24 hours.
  - Rationale: Minimize blast radius and gather real traffic signals.
  - Owner: eng-platform.

Related artifacts and links
- Model onboarding manifest: confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Perf harness and latest results: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- Runtime architecture: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture

How to propose changes
1) Open a PR against this page with clear motivation and impact.
2) If the change affects multiple teams, create an ADR stub (template in architecture-and-standards/decision-records) and circulate to reviewers.
3) For infra or security-affecting changes, notify eng-sre and security-and-compliance and get explicit approval before merging.

Appendix: checklist for new service
- [ ] API contract declared and reviewed (API standards)
- [ ] Unit + integration tests, static typing enforced (Coding standards)
- [ ] Terraform module for infra and least-privilege IAM (Infra standards)
- [ ] Model manifest and fallback variants (Model-serving)
- [ ] OTel tracing + required metrics instrumented (Observability)
- [ ] Perf smoke test added to CI and benchmark results attached (Performance)

Document history
- 2026-07-01: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-07-08: Added ADR-2026-04 (canary-first policy) after eng-platform review.
- 2026-07-15: Finalized SLO examples and published.
